opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly my own journey reflects how that relationship has shifted. I started out very much on the theory side. My early work was on tensor decompositions and spectral methods for learning latent variable models, where the goal was provable guarantees: can we show an algorithm recovers the true parameters efficiently, with a certain number of samples? That was a very satisfying kind of work, because you knew exactly when and why things worked.

Then deep learning took off, and in many ways practice raced ahead of theory. People were training enormous models that worked remarkably well, and our classical theory couldn't fully explain why. Overparameterized networks generalize, non-convex optimization somehow finds good solutions. For a while there was a sense that theory was playing catch-up, or even that it didn't matter as long as the benchmarks went up.

But I've come to see the role of theory differently now. It's less about proving bounds after the fact and more about guiding design, building the right structure into models. Neural operators are a good example. When we wanted to use AI for scientific problems like fluid dynamics, weather, or materials, we couldn't just treat them as image problems on a fixed grid. The underlying physics lives in function spaces, in continuous domains. So we asked, mathematically, what the right object to learn is, and the answer was mappings between functions, operators. That theoretical framing gave us properties like discretization invariance, where you can train at one resolution and evaluate at another. That's not a nice-to-have in science, it's essential.

So I'd say theory has moved from being a gatekeeper to being a compass. In scientific domains especially, you can't just scale up data. Data is expensive, simulations are costly, and you need models that respect physical constraints, conservation laws, and symmetries. That's where mathematical foundations really pay off: they let you be data-efficient and trustworthy, and they let you generalize beyond what you've seen.

And looking ahead, as we push AI toward things like formal reasoning and verifiable mathematics, theory comes back full circle. We want systems whose outputs can be checked rigorously, not just ones that sound plausible. So I think the people who can bridge both worlds, deep mathematical understanding and large-scale engineering, are going to be the ones who make the biggest leaps.

r001.rationale: The response says practice outpaced theory and gives neural operators as an example of theory guiding design, but it does not say unreliable performance in an earlier data-limited phase motivated that role.

r002.rationale: Calling theory a “compass” rather than a “gatekeeper” suggests a changed role, but the response does not clearly argue that theory should not constrain practical exploration.

r003.rationale: The response says scientific problems cannot rely on simply scaling data because data and simulations are costly, but it does not connect saturation in purely data-driven AI to renewed principled design.

r004.rationale: In discussing scientific domains, the response says mathematical foundations help models “generalize beyond what you’ve seen,” conveying extrapolation beyond available data.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I'd say the role of theory has shifted rather than diminished, and in some ways it has become more important.

When I started out, a lot of my work was on tensor methods, spectral algorithms, latent variable models. The appeal was that you could prove something: here are the conditions under which this method recovers the true parameters, here is the sample complexity, here are the guarantees. That was the dominant way of thinking in machine learning at the time. You wanted a clean problem, a clean algorithm, and a proof.

Then deep learning took off, and frankly, the empirical results outran the theory by a wide margin. Networks that theory said should overfit were generalizing. Non-convex optimization that theory said should get stuck was working fine in practice. There was a period where it felt like theory was playing catch-up, trying to explain things after the fact rather than guiding the design.

What I've come to believe is that theory's role is now less about end-to-end guarantees and more about principled design. You may not be able to prove a convergence rate for a large model trained on messy data. But you can ask what structure the problem has, and then build that structure into the architecture or the training. That's very much how I think about our work on neural operators. We're learning mappings between function spaces, solving partial differential equations, and the theory of operators, of resolution invariance, of what it means to approximate a function rather than a vector, directly shaped the architecture. Without that grounding, you're just throwing a convolutional network at a grid and hoping it generalizes to a different resolution, which it won't.

The same thing shows up in physical constraints. If you know a quantity is conserved, or a symmetry holds, theory tells you how to bake that in, and it pays off in data efficiency and reliability. In scientific applications especially, you can't afford a model that's right ninety percent of the time with no idea about the other ten. So the theory matters for trust, not just for understanding.

I'd also say the questions themselves have gotten more interesting. We're now asking what a model has actually learned, whether it has captured the underlying dynamics or just memorized the training distribution, how it behaves out of distribution. Those are deeply theoretical questions, even if the tools to answer them look different from classical learning theory.

So the honest version is that I've become less attached to proofs as the end product and more interested in theory as a lens. It tells you where to look, what to build, and what to be skeptical of. And when the empirical results surprise you, that's where the next theory comes from. The two are in a much tighter loop than they used to be, and I think that's healthy.

r001.rationale: The response says early work emphasized theoretical guarantees, but it does not link unreliable neural-network performance in a data-limited phase to that use of theory.

r002.rationale: It presents theory as a guide for design and skepticism, but does not say theory should not constrain practical exploration.

r003.rationale: It connects theory to principled design, but does not attribute that renewed need to saturation in purely data-driven approaches.

r004.rationale: It discusses out-of-distribution behavior and generalizing across resolutions, but does not characterize scientific discovery as extrapolation beyond available data.

astra-6.text:
For me, theoretical foundations are still essential, but the questions we need theory to answer have changed. Earlier, much of the focus was on analyzing a particular algorithm under well-defined assumptions. With today’s AI systems, there’s a much bigger gap between the settings we can analyze rigorously and what works in practice.

I see that as an opportunity for theory. When something works surprisingly well, can we understand what makes it work? When it fails, can we identify the underlying limitation? Theory should help us choose better architectures, use data more efficiently, and understand when we can trust a model.

This is especially important when we bring AI into scientific problems. We have physical principles and mathematical structure that we can build into the learning process. So I don’t see theory becoming less relevant as models become more powerful. I see a greater need for a dialogue between theory and experiments, where each helps us ask better questions of the other.

r003.rationale: The response calls for incorporating physical principles into scientific AI, but does not connect that need to saturation in purely data-driven approaches.

r004.rationale: It mentions applying AI to scientific problems, but does not characterize scientific discovery as extrapolation beyond available data.

sol-6.1.text:
I see theory as a way to ask better questions, even when it doesn’t yet explain everything we observe. Earlier in my work, the connection was often quite direct: you made assumptions about a problem, designed an algorithm, and proved guarantees. With modern AI, there’s a much bigger gap between what we can prove and what works in practice. That makes the interaction between theory and experimentation especially important.

In scientific machine learning, for example, the foundations help us decide what an architecture should learn. Are we learning a mapping between finite-dimensional vectors, or an operator between functions? That distinction matters when you want a model to work across different resolutions or discretizations.

So I don’t think theory has become less relevant. Its role has broadened: it helps us choose representations, incorporate physical structure, and understand where a model might fail. And the empirical successes give us new mathematical questions to investigate.
